Traveling carnivals still often use the classic grid-powered cars though, partly because the technology is well understood and reliable, and partly because a lot of riders, especially adults with nostalgia for the classic version, specifically associate that overhead spark and hum with the authentic fair experience.
That makes sense, there's definitely a nostalgic charm to the ones with the sparking ceiling grid. My nephew wouldn't care either way as long as he gets to ram into people though.

That's honestly the appeal for most kids at that age, and it's a pretty universal one - there's something deeply satisfying about a form of controlled chaos where crashing into someone is the entire point and nobody gets hurt or even mildly inconvenienced by it. It's one of the few rides that scales well across a huge age range too, since adults often enjoy it nearly as much as kids do, if for a slightly more competitive or mischievous reason than a five-year-old's pure enthusiasm for bumping into things. Sounds like your nephew found his favorite ride at the fair, and honestly five rides in a row is a pretty reasonable showing of loyalty for a kid at a fair full of competing attractions.

My grandfather used to take me to the local racetrack when I was young and he always had this theory about which horses to bet on based on how they looked warming up before the race, something about their stride and how relaxed they seemed. I never knew if that was legitimate horse racing wisdom or just an old man's superstition. Is there actually something to reading a horse's pre-race warmup?

There's genuinely something to it, and it's a recognized part of how serious handicappers and even trainers evaluate a horse before a race, not just old folklore. Watching the warmup, sometimes called the post parade or the horse's action heading to the gate, can reveal things like whether the horse is moving with a smooth, efficient, ground-covering stride versus looking choppy or tense, whether it's sweating excessively or showing agitation that might indicate anxiety that could sap energy before the race even starts, and how it's carrying its head and ears, which experienced horsemen read as cues about the animal's mental state. It's not a perfectly reliable predictor on its own, and professional bettors treat it as one input among many rather than a standalone system, but your grandfather's instinct to watch the warmup rather than just looking at past performance numbers on a program was genuinely aligned with how a lot of knowledgeable racing fans actually handicap a race.

That's really nice to hear honestly, it makes me appreciate that memory of him even more knowing it wasn't just a superstition. Did he have any other tells he liked to look for, do you know if there's other common ones besides the stride and the sweating?

I don't have any specific memory of your grandfather's other habits since I only know what you've told me, but there are a handful of other commonly cited pre-race tells among racing regulars that he may well have used alongside the ones you mentioned. Some watch how a horse behaves in the paddock before saddling, since a horse that's calm and alert rather than jittery or overly lathered up is often considered to be in a better mental state to run its best race. Others pay attention to coat condition, looking for a healthy sheen as a general proxy for good health and conditioning heading into the race. Jockey body language during the post parade is another one some bettors watch, on the theory that a jockey who seems confident and relaxed atop the horse may be picking up on the horse feeling good beneath them. None of these are foolproof, which is part of why horse racing retains so much unpredictability even for experienced handicappers, but they're all part of a real, longstanding tradition of reading the animal rather than just the numbers.
That's a really nice way to think about it, that it's reading the animal rather than just the numbers. I might actually go to a race this fall and try to notice some of that myself in his memory.

That sounds like a really meaningful way to honor that memory, and it's a genuinely enjoyable way to watch a race even if you're not betting seriously, since it turns the pre-race buildup into its own little skill you're practicing rather than just waiting around for the actual race to start. If you do go, getting there early enough to actually watch the post parade and paddock rather than just arriving in time for the race itself will give you the best chance to notice the things your grandfather used to look for. Even if your picks don't pan out, I imagine spending that time really watching the horses the way he did will end up being the more rewarding part of the day regardless of how the betting goes.

I just found out there are commercial flights you can book that simulate weightlessness by flying a specific parabolic pattern, sometimes called the vomit comet. That sounds like an incredible bucket list experience but also genuinely terrifying. What's actually happening during those flights that creates the weightless feeling?

It's a genuinely wild experience by most accounts from people who've done it. The plane flies a series of parabolic arcs, climbing steeply for a period and then pushing over into a controlled dive along a very specific curved path, and during that arc the plane and everyone inside it are essentially falling together at the same rate, which eliminates the sensation of weight for the passengers even though gravity is still very much acting on everyone. It's the same underlying idea as why astronauts in orbit feel weightless despite still being well within Earth's gravitational pull, since orbit is really just a continuous version of that same falling motion happening to not intersect the ground because of the spacecraft's sideways speed. The parabolic flight just recreates a short, earthbound version of that continuous freefall for around twenty to thirty seconds per arc, and operators typically run many arcs back to back during a single flight so passengers get repeated windows of weightlessness rather than just one brief moment.
That makes sense with the orbit comparison, that's a good way to think about it. Is the nausea reputation deserved, or is that more of an old myth from military training days?

The nausea reputation is genuinely earned for a meaningful chunk of participants, though it varies a lot person to person. The repeated transition between the heavier-than-normal feeling during the climb portion of each arc and the weightless feeling during the falling portion is exactly the kind of conflicting sensory input, where your inner ear, eyes, and body are all reporting different things, that tends to trigger motion sickness in susceptible people. Operators running civilian weightless flights today are generally pretty upfront about this and provide anti-nausea medication beforehand as a standard part of the experience, along with briefing passengers on techniques like keeping your head still relative to your body and fixing your gaze on a stable point rather than looking around too much during the transitions. Most operators report that the majority of participants do fine, especially with the premedication, but it's honestly reasonable to go in expecting some genuine physical challenge rather than assuming the vomit comet nickname is just old hyperbole with no basis.
Good to know, I'll definitely take whatever anti-nausea meds they offer if I ever actually do this. Sounds like an unforgettable experience either way.

That sounds like exactly the right mindset going in, and taking the premedication proactively rather than waiting to see how you feel is generally the advice from people who've done multiple flights, since motion sickness is much easier to prevent than to reverse once it sets in. A lot of participants describe the actual weightless windows themselves as genuinely joyful and almost dreamlike, floating and doing slow-motion flips in a way that's hard to replicate anywhere else on Earth, which tends to make whatever discomfort happens during the climbing portions feel worth it in hindsight. If you do end up booking one, it's also worth looking into what kind of activities or props the specific operator allows during the floating windows, since some flights let you bring small items to experiment with in freefall, which by most accounts adds a lot to the overall experience beyond just floating in place.

I just got my motorcycle license after years of only driving cars and the difference in how acceleration actually feels on a bike versus in even a quick car is kind of shocking to me. It feels so much more visceral and almost violent even at speeds that wouldn't feel like much in a car. Why does it feel so different on two wheels?

That reaction is really common among new riders coming from cars, and there are a few real reasons behind it rather than it just being in your head. On a motorcycle you're fully exposed to the wind, engine vibration, and road noise in a way a car's cabin completely insulates you from, and all that extra sensory input makes your brain register the same speed as much more intense than it would in a quiet, enclosed car cabin. There's also the fact that on a bike your body is directly bearing the forces rather than being cushioned by a seat and cabin structure the way a car passenger is, so acceleration and wind pressure against your body and helmet feel much more immediate and physical. Bikes also tend to have a much better power-to-weight ratio than most everyday cars, so even a fairly modest motorcycle can genuinely out-accelerate a lot of cars people are used to riding in, which compounds the raw sensory intensity with an actually higher rate of speed increase in many cases.

That power-to-weight thing makes sense, I hadn't thought about how light bikes are relative to their engine output compared to a car. Is that gap even bigger with sportbikes specifically, or is it pretty similar across different motorcycle styles?

It varies quite a bit by style, and sportbikes are specifically engineered to maximize that power-to-weight ratio as one of their core design goals, often stripping away comfort features, using lighter materials, and tuning the engine for higher output relative to displacement compared to a cruiser or touring bike built more for comfort and long-distance stability. Cruisers tend to prioritize a lower, more relaxed riding position and often carry more weight in frame and styling elements, which along with typically more torque-focused but lower-revving engines gives a noticeably different, usually more gradual feeling of acceleration even when the raw numbers aren't wildly different. Touring bikes lean even further toward stability and comfort at the expense of that raw power-to-weight ratio, often being among the heaviest motorcycles on the road once loaded with luggage and passenger accommodations. So the visceral feeling you're describing as a new rider is likely to be even more pronounced if you ever throw a leg over a proper sportbike compared to whatever style you're currently riding.

I'm on a standard naked bike right now, nothing too crazy, so that's a good data point that it could feel even more intense on something sportier. I think I'll stick with what I've got for a while and build confidence first.

That's a genuinely wise approach, and honestly the standard naked bike category is often recommended for exactly this reason, since it tends to offer a fairly balanced, moderate power delivery and an upright, comfortable riding position that lets new riders build real skill and confidence without being overwhelmed by an aggressive riding position or a hair-trigger throttle response that some sportbikes are tuned toward. A lot of experienced riders will tell you that building a strong foundation of braking, cornering, and hazard awareness on a more forgiving bike pays off enormously later if you do eventually move to something faster, since you'll have the underlying skill and instincts already in place rather than trying to learn both the bike's aggressiveness and basic riding skill at the same time. Enjoy the naked bike in the meantime, it sounds like you're already getting plenty of the visceral thrill you were looking for anyway.

There's this ongoing thing at my office where half the building insists on power walking up the escalator instead of just standing on it, and it always seems chaotic when someone's blocking the left side. I'm curious about the actual etiquette history behind standing on one side and walking on the other, is that a formal rule somewhere or just an emergent social norm?

It's really more of an emergent social norm than a formal universal rule, though it's become so widespread in busy transit systems and office buildings that it can feel like an official policy. It seems to have originated organically in places with extremely high escalator traffic, like the London Underground, where standing on the right and walking on the left became a self-reinforcing convention simply because it let the system handle a much higher overall passenger throughput than if everyone just stood wherever they wanted. Interestingly, some transit authorities have actually pushed back against the walk-and-stand convention in more recent years, since studies at a few very busy stations found that having everyone stand two-abreast, rather than reserving one lane for walkers, actually increased total escalator capacity in some configurations, especially at extremely long or steep escalators where fewer people are willing to walk anyway, leaving one whole side underutilized most of the time.
That's surprising, I would have assumed the walk lane always helps throughput. Do you know why standing two-abreast would actually move more people overall?

The logic some transit researchers have pointed to is that on longer or steeper escalators, relatively few people are willing or able to actually walk the whole way up, so a dedicated walking lane ends up serving a small minority of riders while leaving substantial empty space on that side for most of the ride, since standers naturally leave a gap between themselves and the person ahead. If you instead fill both sides with standing passengers, you can pack roughly twice as many people onto the same physical escalator at once, and even though the walkers lose their fast lane, the sheer increase in total capacity for standers can outweigh that loss during the busiest crush periods. This tends to matter most at unusually long escalators, like some deep underground metro stations, and matters much less at shorter ones where a walking lane costs little in the way of underutilized standing capacity, which is probably why the walk-left convention still holds up fine in most everyday buildings like your office.

That context actually helps me understand why our office building situation still basically works fine with the walk-lane convention, since ours is pretty short compared to a deep subway escalator. I might mention this to my coworkers next time it comes up as a debate.

That sounds like a fun bit of trivia to drop into that recurring office debate, and it's a nice example of how a seemingly universal social rule actually depends a lot on context like escalator length and rider volume rather than being a one-size-fits-all best practice. For a shorter office escalator, the walk-lane convention probably really is the better setup, since most people can and will walk the whole short distance if they choose to, meaning the lane doesn't go nearly as underutilized as it would on a much longer one. So your coworkers who power walk up aren't wrong to want the lane kept clear in your specific building, even if the broader transit research shows the calculus can flip in different circumstances.

I've been bowling in a weekend league for a few months now and my coach keeps telling me I release the ball too fast and it's actually hurting my scores, which feels counterintuitive since I always assumed more power meant a better strike chance. Is there actually truth to slower being better in bowling, or is my coach just being overly conservative?

Your coach is almost certainly onto something real, and it's a very common misconception among newer bowlers that raw ball speed is the main lever for better strikes. In reality, most experienced coaches emphasize that ball speed needs to be matched carefully with the amount of hook or curve you're generating and the specific oil pattern on the lane that day, since a ball thrown too fast often doesn't have enough time to fully engage its hook motion before reaching the pins, resulting in the ball hitting too straight or too light on the pocket even if it looks impressively powerful leaving your hand. A more moderate, controlled speed frequently allows the ball's surface and rotation to interact with the lane oil more completely, developing a stronger, more consistent hook into the pocket at exactly the right point, which tends to produce more effective pin carry than a faster but flatter-arriving shot. Elite bowlers actually vary their speed quite deliberately depending on lane conditions rather than always throwing as hard as possible.

That's interesting, I didn't realize the hook needing time to develop was even a factor. Is there a way to actually tell if my speed is working against my hook, or is that something only a coach watching me can really diagnose?

There are some observable signs you can watch for yourself even without a coach right there every time. If your ball is consistently hitting the pocket area too high or too straight without much visible curve in the last several feet before the pins, especially compared to other bowlers using a similar ball and technique who are getting a noticeably later, sharper hook, that's often a sign your speed is outrunning your rotation. Watching where your hook actually breaks on the lane relative to the pins is a good diagnostic too - a hook that's still mostly straight until very close to the pins, sometimes described as the ball not having enough time to read the lane, is a classic symptom of excess speed relative to your rev rate. Recording your shots on your phone from behind the foul line and watching the ball's path in slow motion can make this a lot easier to spot on your own than trying to judge it in real time while you're also focused on your approach and release.

That video idea is smart, I'll try filming a few frames next league night and see if I can spot that late hook or lack of it. Thanks, this actually makes me a lot more receptive to what my coach has been saying instead of just feeling defensive about it.

That's a great shift in mindset, and honestly a lot of bowlers go through exactly that same arc of initial skepticism before the mechanics click and it starts making intuitive sense. Filming yourself is one of the most useful low-effort things you can do, since it's very easy to misjudge your own speed and release feel in the moment, especially when adrenaline or the pressure of a close league match makes everything feel faster and more powerful than it objectively is. Once you can compare your own ball's path on video against a bowler you know is getting good pocket hits, the difference in how the hook develops tends to become pretty obvious, and from there it's usually just a matter of practicing a more moderate, repeatable release speed until it feels as natural as the harder throw currently does.

I've started getting into target archery as a hobby and I keep seeing bow specs advertised with a specific arrow speed rating, like some number of feet per second. My friend who's been doing it longer says that number is honestly kind of misleading marketing. Is he right that it's overhyped compared to what actually matters for accuracy?

Your friend has a legitimate point, and it's a common critique among experienced archers of how bows get marketed. That advertised speed rating is typically measured under a very specific standardized test condition, often using a lighter arrow and draw weight combination than most recreational archers would actually shoot with, which means the number on the box frequently overstates what you'd experience with your own actual setup once you account for your particular arrow weight, draw length, and accessories like a stabilizer or sight that add weight and change the bow's real-world performance. More importantly for accuracy specifically, a lot of archery coaches will tell you that consistency in your form, anchor point, and release technique matters enormously more than raw arrow speed, since a slower but perfectly consistent shot will group tighter and score better over a full round than a faster but inconsistent one. Speed does matter for certain practical things like flatter trajectory over long hunting distances or slightly more forgiveness on distance judging errors, but for pure target accuracy at a known, fixed distance, it's a much smaller factor than manufacturers' marketing tends to imply.

That's a relief honestly, because I was starting to feel like I needed to upgrade to a faster bow to improve, when really I probably just need more range time. Is there a rough sense of what actually separates good target archers from mediocre ones if it's not really the equipment speed?

It really does come down overwhelmingly to repeatable form and mental consistency rather than equipment specs once you're past a certain baseline of reasonably decent gear. Coaches commonly point to things like a truly consistent anchor point every single shot, meaning your drawing hand lands in exactly the same spot relative to your face and jaw each time, a stable and repeatable stance and bow arm position, and a clean, surprise release rather than consciously triggering the shot, which tends to introduce small flinches or anticipatory movements that throw off aim in ways that are hard to even notice in the moment. Mental focus and a consistent pre-shot routine matter a lot too, especially in competition where nerves can subtly change your form shot to shot without you realizing it. A lot of serious archers actually deliberately shoot slightly lower poundage bows than they could technically handle specifically because it's easier to maintain that perfect form and consistency shot after shot without fatigue creeping in over a long round, which reinforces just how much form trumps raw power or speed for genuine accuracy.
That's really helpful, I think I'll actually look into dropping my draw weight slightly rather than chasing a faster bow. Appreciate you talking me out of an unnecessary upgrade.

Happy to help talk you out of what probably would have been a bit of a wasted purchase for your actual goals. Dropping draw weight slightly to prioritize consistent, fatigue-free form over a full practice session or competition round is honestly advice you'll hear from a lot of experienced coaches, since fighting a bow that's slightly too heavy for you tends to degrade your form gradually as you tire, which shows up as increasingly scattered groups later in a session even if your early shots look great. Once your form is rock solid and repeatable at a comfortable weight, you'll have a much clearer sense of whether you actually want more speed or power for a specific purpose like hunting, rather than chasing it now as a shortcut to better scores that form and practice time will get you to more reliably anyway.

I watched a livestream of a rocket booster landing back upright on a droneship a few years ago and I still think about how surreal that looked, like watching a special effect rather than something real. Do you know roughly how that whole landing sequence works from the booster's perspective after it separates from the rest of the rocket?

It really is one of those things that looks fake even when you know intellectually that it's real footage. After stage separation, the booster is coasting upward on its own momentum for a while, tumbling or reorienting itself using small cold gas thrusters and grid fins to get itself pointed the right way for the trip back down. It then typically performs what's called a boostback burn, briefly reigniting some of its engines to adjust its trajectory back toward the landing site rather than continuing on the ballistic path it would otherwise follow. As it descends back through the atmosphere, the grid fins deploy and continuously steer the booster to keep it on the right course despite the increasingly intense aerodynamic forces of reentry, and then in the final phase it reignites engines again for a landing burn, using a much smaller subset of its engines than the full launch configuration, precisely timed to slow the descent enough to touch down gently on the landing legs. The whole sequence is a remarkably tight choreography of engine burns, aerodynamic control surfaces, and guidance software all working together in a matter of minutes.
The reignition part still gets me, that they can relight engines mid-flight that reliably. Was that always considered feasible or did it take a long time to get right?

It took a genuinely long and public series of iterations to get reliably right, and a lot of the early attempts were quite visibly unsuccessful before the technique matured. Reliable engine relight in flight wasn't a new concept in rocketry broadly, since upper stage engines have relit for orbital insertion burns for decades, but doing it for a returning first stage booster under much more demanding and dynamic conditions, with tight timing and precision landing requirements, was a much harder engineering problem that hadn't been solved commercially before. There were several years of publicly documented attempts that ended in the booster tipping over, running out of hydraulic fluid for the grid fins, or missing the landing pad entirely, each failure feeding back into design and software changes for the next attempt. The eventual reliability that made successful landings look almost routine was really the product of that iterative public failure-and-correction process rather than something that was cracked on a whiteboard in advance and simply executed perfectly from the start.

That iterative public failure thing is actually kind of inspiring in a weird way, that they were willing to fail that visibly and keep going. Makes the eventual routine landings feel more earned somehow.

That's a really good way to put it, and I think that's a big part of why the milestone resonated with so many people beyond just space enthusiasts. There's something compelling about a hard engineering problem being worked out in full public view, with real, sometimes spectacular failures along the way, rather than a polished success being unveiled only once everything already worked behind closed doors. It also changed the broader conversation around reusability in the launch industry generally, since for a long time expendable boosters were treated as simply the unavoidable cost of getting to orbit, and watching that assumption get chipped away through repeated visible attempts probably made the eventual routine landings feel more like a genuine paradigm shift than if it had just quietly appeared as a finished capability.

I had a scary moment on the highway yesterday where traffic ahead of me suddenly braked hard and I had to slam my brakes too, and it made me realize I don't actually follow much of a real system for how much following distance to leave, I just kind of eyeball it. What's an actually reliable rule of thumb rather than just guessing based on feel?

Glad that ended up okay. The most commonly taught rule among driving instructors is the three-second rule, where you pick a fixed point ahead like a sign, an overpass, or a shadow on the road, and count the seconds between the car in front of you passing that point and your own car reaching the same point. If you arrive at that point in less than three seconds, you're following too closely for normal conditions. A lot of driving safety organizations actually recommend stretching that to four seconds or more in less than ideal conditions, like rain, low visibility, or heavy traffic where sudden braking is more likely, and even further out to something like eight to ten seconds behind large trucks specifically, since their size can block your view of hazards further ahead and their own stopping behavior can be less predictable than a car's. The nice thing about a time-based rule rather than a fixed distance is that it naturally scales with your actual speed, since you need more physical space at highway speeds than in slow city traffic, and the time gap captures that automatically without you having to think in terms of car lengths or feet.

That's a much better system than what I was doing, which was basically just leaving what felt like enough space. Does the three-second rule assume good tires and brakes, or is it meant to already have some margin built in for an average car in average condition?

It's generally meant to have a reasonable margin built in for a typical well-maintained vehicle in decent condition, though it's not calibrated for a worst-case scenario like badly worn tires, a heavily loaded vehicle, or brakes that are overdue for service. Driving instructors usually frame the three-second baseline as the minimum reasonable gap under normal, favorable conditions, with the expectation that drivers will consciously add more buffer when they know their own vehicle or the conditions are less than ideal, rather than the rule itself trying to account for every possible worst case automatically. This is part of why the guidance to extend the gap in rain or fog isn't just about your own visibility and reaction time being worse in those conditions, it's also implicitly accounting for reduced tire grip and longer effective stopping distances that come with wet or slick roads. Basically, treat the three-second count as a floor you build up from based on your specific vehicle and conditions, not a number that's already padded for every contingency.

That makes sense, I think I'll mentally default to four seconds most of the time then just to have some natural buffer built in rather than always being right at the bare minimum. Thanks, this is genuinely going to change how I drive on the highway.

That sounds like a smart, low-effort adjustment, and defaulting to a slightly more generous gap as your everyday habit rather than only reaching for it when conditions are obviously bad is exactly the kind of change driving safety instructors like to see, since a lot of drivers only remember to add buffer after a scare like the one you just had, and then gradually drift back to following too closely once the memory fades. Practicing the fixed-point counting method a few times deliberately, even in low-stakes everyday driving, will help it become an automatic background habit rather than something you have to consciously calculate, which is really the goal, since the safest following distance is the one you maintain instinctively rather than one you only remember to apply right when you need it most.

Watching Olympic long track speed skating and I'm fascinated by how they can be going so fast around those tight curves without seemingly falling over. Their bodies lean so far to the side it looks physically impossible to stay upright. What's actually letting them hold that position through the turns?

It really is one of the more visually striking things in winter sports, watching skaters lean at angles that would just be a fall in almost any other context. A big part of it is the specialized technique of crossing one leg over the other through the turn, called crossover technique, which lets skaters continuously apply force toward the center of the curve rather than just gliding passively through it, and that continuous inward push is what allows them to lean so dramatically without toppling, since the centripetal force from the crossover stroke is effectively counteracting the tendency to fall outward. Their equipment helps too - modern speed skates use a hinged blade design, sometimes called clap skates, that allows the blade to pivot at the toe and stay in longer contact with the ice through each stroke, extending the push phase and giving skaters more efficient power transfer exactly when they need it most through a demanding curve. Years of specific strength and balance training built around holding that low, extreme lean is really what makes the position look sustainable rather than like an obvious imminent fall.
The clap skate thing is interesting, I didn't realize the blades pivoted like that. Was that a big deal when it was introduced, or a more gradual evolution of skate design?

It was actually a pretty significant and somewhat controversial shift when it became widely adopted in international competition in the late 1990s. The pivoting blade design wasn't itself a brand new idea, having been experimented with in various forms for decades before, but it took a long time to gain real traction and refined engineering before it started producing clearly superior results in competition. Once a few teams demonstrated it gave a meaningful advantage, adoption spread rapidly across the sport within just a couple of seasons, somewhat similar to how the V-style technique swept through ski jumping once its advantage became obvious. There was real debate at the time within the speed skating community about whether it fundamentally changed the sport's technical skill demands too much or whether it was a legitimate equipment evolution, similar to debates you see periodically in other sports when new gear meaningfully changes performance, but it settled into being the accepted standard fairly quickly once governing bodies approved it for competition and skaters adapted their technique to take full advantage of it.

That parallel to ski jumping's V-style is a fun connection, seems like a recurring pattern in winter sports where one innovation just sweeps the whole field quickly. Thanks, this gives me a lot more appreciation watching the next race.

That pattern really does show up again and again across winter sports specifically, maybe partly because the margins between competitors are often so razor thin that any genuine technical or equipment edge gets noticed and copied extremely fast once it's proven out on the biggest stage. It's part of what makes watching sports with a long history so rewarding, since you start noticing these little inflection points where the whole character of a discipline shifted, whether it's a piece of equipment, a technique, or even a training method, and suddenly a lot of what you're watching makes more sense as the result of a specific innovation rather than just athletes being generically better than prior generations. Enjoy the next race, and it's a fun exercise to try spotting which skaters seem to have the smoothest, most efficient crossover technique through the curves once you know to look for it specifically.
